This site builds the same deck twice, from the same front matter:

- [with the filter](preview.html);
- [without it](preview-without.html).

Viewing the source of each, or fetching them, shows what the filter changes.

![](preview.html){.embed-art loading="lazy" title="The deck built with the filter" style="--atelier-embed-art-ratio: 1.78;"}

## What Quarto emits by itself

Rendering the deck with no filter at all produces twelve tags:

```txt
og:title             og:description       og:image         og:image:alt
og:locale            og:site_name         twitter:card     twitter:title
twitter:description  twitter:image        twitter:creator  twitter:image:alt
```

That is more than the README of this extension assumed, and enough for most previews.

## What the filter adds

Seven tags Quarto does not write for a deck:

| Tag | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| `description` | The ordinary HTML description, which a deck otherwise has no meta tag for. |
| `og:url` | One of the four properties the Open Graph protocol requires. |
| `og:type` | Another of them. Falls back to `website`. |
| `og:image:width`, `og:image:height` | Let a scraper lay the card out before fetching the image. |
| `og:image:type` | Inferred from the file extension. |
| `og:image:secure_url` | Added when the image URL is HTTPS. |

: The tags only the filter writes. {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[38,62]"}

## What is written twice

Running both leaves ten tags in the head twice, once from Quarto and once from the filter:

```txt
og:title  og:description  og:image  og:locale  og:site_name
twitter:card  twitter:title  twitter:description  twitter:image  twitter:creator
```

Eight of those ten carry the same value twice.
The deck sets `lang: en-GB`, and the two `og:locale` tags disagree on it: Quarto rewrites the value into the underscored `en_GB` the Open Graph protocol specifies, while the filter passes it through as `en-GB`.
The two `og:site_name` tags disagree as well, because Quarto takes the site title and the filter takes the value given under `open-graph.site-name`.

The filter writes its block ahead of Quarto's, so for each duplicated property its copy is the first one in the head.

::: {.callout-note}
The deck sets `image-alt` at the top level, which Quarto reads and the filter does not, so `og:image:alt` and `twitter:image:alt` come from Quarto alone.
Setting it under `open-graph.image-alt` instead puts it within the filter's reach.
:::

## Where each value comes from

The [Reference](reference.qmd#metadata-resolution) has the full resolution order.
In short: the standard Quarto keys are read first, and `extensions.social` is the fallback for anything they cannot express.

The deck above sets no `extensions.social` options at all, which is the usual case.

## Source

The repository ships a short, standalone starting point you can copy: [`example.qmd`](https://github.com/mcanouil/quarto-revealjs-social/blob/main/example.qmd).
